title: Short Form Video for Apartment Communities: What to Film and How to Measure It
seoTitle: Short Form Video for Apartments: What to Film
seoDescription: What apartment communities should film for Instagram Reels, TikTok and YouTube Shorts, how long videos should be, and how to measure them past views.
excerpt: Film what a floor plan cannot show, keep most videos under a minute, and judge them by what renters do after the view.
imageAlt: Man filming himself in a living room with a smartphone mounted on a handheld gimbal in the foreground
imageIdea: Real photo of someone filming vertical video on a phone inside an apartment, daylight, no brand logos.
author: Michael Shad, Founder of The SocialDM
bodyHtml:
Film the things a renter cannot judge from a floor plan: the walk from parking to the front door, the light in a real unit, the amenities at the hour people actually use them, and the people who work there. Then measure each video by what it does for leasing, such as profile visits, website clicks and tours, not by views alone.

Short form video is one of the few places a community can show what living there feels like. Done well, it answers questions before a renter calls. Done badly, it is a trend audio over a drone shot that tells nobody anything.

Why does short form video matter for an apartment community?

Because photos and floor plans leave out the questions renters care about most: how big the unit feels, how far the walk is, how loud the pool deck gets. A 30 second clip answers those faster than a paragraph, and the same clip works across Instagram Reels, TikTok and YouTube Shorts.

The platforms have also made room for longer vertical video. YouTube announced that from October 15, 2024, creators could upload Shorts up to three minutes long. Instagram said in January 2025 that it was raising the reel limit to three minutes for creators in the U.S. Longer is allowed. That does not mean longer is better, which I come back to below.

What should a property team film first?

Start with the questions your leasing team answers every day. If the same question comes up on five tours a week, it deserves a video. These are the clips I would build first, roughly in this order.

  • The arrival. Parking or the garage, the walk to the leasing office, and the walk to a typical unit door. Renters want to know the real distance.
  • One real unit, room by room. Natural light, the view from the window, closet and storage space, the kitchen with cabinets open. Shoot it in the daytime and do not overdress it.
  • Amenities in use. The gym at 7 a.m., the pool on a Saturday, the package room at 5 p.m. Empty amenities shot at noon look like a brochure.
  • The neighborhood. The coffee shop around the corner, the walk to transit, the grocery store. Show actual distances, not adjectives.
  • The team. A leasing agent answering one common question in plain words, or maintenance explaining how to submit a work order. People rent from people.
  • Policy explainers. Pets, parking, package delivery and move in steps. Short, factual and easy to update when a policy changes.

Our earlier post on authentic social media for Class A properties covers the tone side of this. The short version: real beats polished, but real still needs to be in focus and well lit.

How long should apartment videos be?

Most should be under 60 seconds, with the answer in the first few seconds. Use the longer limits only for full unit tours or walkthroughs where the viewer has chosen to watch.

One reason to stay at three minutes or less on Instagram: its creator FAQ says it recommends videos to people who do not follow you only when they are three minutes or less. Shorts and TikTok do not need a different cut, so I usually film once and edit one short version and one longer tour.

Who should appear on camera, and what permissions do you need?

Team members who are comfortable on camera, with written consent, and residents only with a signed release. Never film a resident, their unit, their car or their door without permission, and keep unit numbers, faces in windows and mail out of frame.

Have your legal contact approve a simple release form and a short list of what is never filmed. If a video is about who lives at the community rather than what the community offers, run it past your fair housing training before it posts. Show the place and the amenities, and let every renter picture themselves there.

Do you need different videos for Reels, TikTok and Shorts?

Usually not. Shoot vertical, keep text away from the edges where each app puts its buttons, and export a clean file from your own editor for each platform. What changes is the caption and the first line of text on screen.

I would write captions the way renters search: the neighborhood, the unit type, the question the video answers. A caption like "Two bedroom tour near downtown, with the walk to the light rail" is more useful than three emojis and a slogan.

How should you measure short form video?

Measure each video by what it does after the view: watch time, shares and saves, profile visits, link clicks and, where you can trace them, tours. Views alone are a weak signal. YouTube, for one, now counts a Shorts view the moment it starts to play.

YouTube changed how Shorts views are counted from March 31, 2025, to every start or replay with no minimum watch time, and kept the older measure as "engaged views." A big view count can therefore mean a lot of people scrolled past. Instagram also moved to Views as its primary metric across formats in 2024, according to Meta's developer update, so check how each platform defines the number before you compare them.

MetricWhat it tells you
ViewsReach, loosely. Useful for comparing your own videos, not much else
Average watch time or engaged viewsWhether people stayed for the answer
Shares and savesWhether a renter wanted to show someone or come back later
Profile visits and link clicksWhether the video moved someone toward leasing
Website sessions from tagged linksTraffic you can follow into tour requests
"How did you hear about us" on the guest cardA rough but direct read on whether video shows up in tours

Tag every link in a bio or caption so your website analytics can tell which platform sent the visit. Our post on multifamily marketing metrics covers how to tie those numbers to leases.

How often should a community post?

As often as the team can keep it up with real footage. One or two useful videos a week, every week, beats a burst of ten in a month and then silence. Batch filming helps: one morning of shooting can cover several weeks.

Video also feeds the rest of your visibility. The same clips can go on your Google Business Profile and website, where renters and search engines can find them. That cross channel view is how we approach social at The SocialDM as a multifamily marketing agency.

Questions we hear

What should an apartment community film first?

Start with the questions your leasing team answers most: the walk from parking, a real unit room by room, amenities in use, the neighborhood and policy explainers like pets and parking.

How long should apartment Reels, TikToks and Shorts be?

Most should be under 60 seconds with the answer up front. Instagram says it recommends videos to non followers only when they are three minutes or less, so keep longer tours within that.

Do we need separate videos for each platform?

Usually not. Shoot vertical, keep text away from the edges, export a clean file from your editor for each platform, and change the caption to match how renters search.

Are views a good way to judge our videos?

Not on their own. YouTube counts a Shorts view as soon as it starts to play, with no minimum watch time, so look at watch time, shares, saves, profile visits, link clicks and tours.

Can we feature residents in our videos?

Only with a signed release your legal contact has approved. Keep unit numbers, mail and anyone who has not agreed out of frame.

takeaways: Film the things a floor plan cannot show, such as the walk from parking, a real unit and amenities in use.
Keep most videos under 60 seconds, and keep longer tours to three minutes or less, the limit Instagram gives for recommending videos to non followers.
